title_en: Sony brings AI upscaling to the base PS5
title_fa: Sony brings AI upscaling to the base PS5
excerpt_en: Marvel's Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei are the first games to support Quick Spectral Super Resolution.
excerpt_fa: Marvel's Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei are the first games to support Quick Spectral Super Resolution.
content_en:
Sony brings AI upscaling to the base PS5
Marvel’s Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei are the first games to support Quick Spectral Super Resolution.
Sony Interactive Entertainment has added AI upscaling to the standard PS5. It's deploying patches for Marvel's Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei today that make them the first games to support Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR) through new graphics options. SIE said the tech delivers "notable improvements" to image detail and stability, adding that every PlayStation developer will be able to add QSSR to their games.
The company has offered PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) upscaling on PS5 Pro since the higher-end version of the console arrived two years ago and it has continued to iterate on the tech. In a blog post, Sony says players and developers asked whether it was possible to bring a similar option to the less-powerful PS5.
QSSR stems from a project that Sony worked on with AMD. It says it's now able to offer AI upscaling on PS5 thanks to "a streamlined neural network architecture" and "a hand-tuned implementation that maximizes performance."
Mike Fitzgerald, head of technology at Wolverine developer Insomniac Games, said the tech "adds more pixel-level clarity and stability to our environments, bringing out extra detail amidst the busy streets of Madripoor, the dense alleyways of Shinjuku and many other areas across Logan's epic journey."
QSSR is arriving on Ghost of Yōtei on the same day Sucker Punch Productions is releasing a complete edition for that game with a story expansion and a roguelike mode that's akin to The Last of Us Part 2's No Return. Folks who already own the game can upgrade for $15.

Mike Fitzgerald, head of technology at Wolverine developer Insomniac Games, said the tech "adds more pixel-level clarity and stability to our environments, bringing out extra detail amidst the busy streets of Madripoor, the dense alleyways of Shinjuku and many other areas across Logan's epic journey."
QSSR is arriving on Ghost of Yōtei on the same day Sucker Punch Productions is releasing a complete edition for that game with a story expansion and a roguelike mode that's akin to The Last of Us Part 2's No Return. Folks who already own the game can upgrade for $15.

title_en: Samsung Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra vs Galaxy Tab S11 Ultra: The difference one year can make
title_fa: Samsung Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra vs Galaxy Tab S11 Ultra: The difference one year can make
excerpt_en: An iterative upgrade once again for Samsung's laptop-sized tablet line.
excerpt_fa: An iterative upgrade once again for Samsung's laptop-sized tablet line.
content_en:
Samsung Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra vs Galaxy Tab S11 Ultra: The difference one year can make
An iterative upgrade once again for Samsung's laptop-sized tablet line.
Holding up the newly announced Samsung Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra alongside its predecessor from last year, the Galaxy Tab S11 Ultra, you'd be hard pressed to spot a physical difference. The biggest and baddest of Samsung's Android tablets is still a comically large and impossibly thin slab of glass, still rocking a 14.6" AMOLED display to make it a media consumption and productivity powerhouse.
It's an iterative update from Samsung, in other words, which has been the case with every tablet in its oversized, top-end lineup. But why mess with a working formula after this many refinements? Aside from removing the ability to remote control your tablet with an S Pen, which was not brought back this time around, the Tab S11 Ultra changed very little compared to the Tab S10 Ultra, and the new Tab S12 Ultra doesn't even look that different from the original Tab S8 Ultra released over four years ago. Tablets are tablets, and it's mostly what's under the hood that makes this year's upgrade worth examining.
The Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra's modest processor upgrade comes with a massive price hike
The Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra's laptop-sized display is once again interrupted only by a teardrop camera cutout for its single, ultra-wide lens — a serviceable selfie and video call camera at 12 megapixels. As for the display itself, it's a 2,960 by 1,848 pixel Dynamic AMOLED 2X panel, just like every other tablet before it in this lineup including the S11 Ultra. This year, peak brightness sits at 1,600 nits for HDR content and 1,000 nits in high brightness mode, same as last year. The panels Samsung uses for this line of oversized tablets have always been impressive, and if you haven't held one in your hands, you're missing out on some true eye candy. Engadget's review of the S12 Ultra confirms that hasn't changed.
One solid upgrade this time around is support for four-channel spatial audio using the onboard four-speaker array. That's up from 2-channel spatial audio on the last-generation tablet. I can confirm that the four-speaker array on Samsung's previous Ultra tablets are second only to their displays in terms of wow factor. Watching TV and movies, especially those with good spatial mixes, I've experienced surprisingly wide soundstages and element positioning.
There is, predictably, a chip upgrade from the MediaTek Dimensity 9300+ to the Dimensity 9500 inside the S12 Ultra. Like its predecessor, the chip is built on a 3nm process. Samsung claims it represents a 19 percent increase in CPU performance and a 17 percent increase in GPU power, along with a 61 percent jump in NPU (if you're doing heavy AI tasks on your Samsung tablet, please explain what and why). There's also a new 3D vapor chamber for heat dissipation. But as 2nm mobile chips finally make major inroads into the market with the recent Apple A20 Pro and Qualcomm 8 Elite Gen 6 bringing major performance gains to the table, this processor doesn't bring enough uplift to justify the tablet's equally increased price. As is tradition at this point in the RAM-aggedon crisis, the Tab S12 Ultra starts at $1,400 for the 256 GB model with 12 GB of RAM. That's a price hike of $200 over the launch price commanded by the S11 Ultra. You'd be hard pressed to find a more expensive Android tablet from a mainstream vendor.
Samsung isn't fixing what's not broken on the Tab S12 Ultra
Sadly, there's no increase to the charging speed, which remains at 45W for the 11,600 milliamp-hour battery, which is also the same size found on the S11 Ultra. In a landscape where more nimble competitors like Redmagic are putting out tablets like the Astra 2 with much speedier charging (to say nothing of other specs), it's a bit of a letdown to see Samsung stagnate here. Again, the higher price would go down with more honey had we seen some real upgrades.
The two tablets are otherwise almost entirely identical. S12 Ultra will ship with the latest One UI 9.0 Android skin out of the box, but the S11 Ultra will get the same update before too long. Both tablets have the same IP68 water and dust resistance rating, so if you want to watch Netflix in the pool, either one will do. Both tablets have the same exact body measurements, the same thickness at 5.1 millimeters and even the same weight down to the gram — 692 grams to be precise.
If you skipped out on the Galaxy Tab S11 Ultra because of its paltry updates compared to the S10 Ultra, there's very little here to compel you this time around. If you've felt stymied by the performance of the S11 Ultra, you won't get a lot more breathing room from the new chip, and even S10 Ultra owners may not have a compelling reason to upgrade. If you've still got an S9 Ultra or even an S8 Ultra, this will feel like a significant boost, but the price is still difficult to swallow. Samsung didn't release the Tab S12 Ultra with any great fanfare, and nor should it have — a press release launch for an on-paper update. Even so, you're not going to find a more well-specced Android tablet at this size.

title_en: Sony brings AI graphics upscaling to the regular PS5
title_fa: Sony brings AI graphics upscaling to the regular PS5
excerpt_en: Sony is launching a new AI upscaling technology specifically for the regular PS5. The new tech, called Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR), is a "new performance tier of AI upscaling" that's a result of Sony's Project Amethyst work with AMD, according to a blog post. Sony...
excerpt_fa: Sony is launching a new AI upscaling technology specifically for the regular PS5. The new tech, called Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR), is a "new performance tier of AI upscaling" that's a result of Sony's Project Amethyst work with AMD, according to a blog post. Sony...
content_en:
Sony is launching a new AI upscaling technology specifically for the regular PS5. The new tech, called Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR), is a “new performance tier of AI upscaling” that’s a result of Sony’s Project Amethyst work with AMD, according to a blog post.
Sony brings AI graphics upscaling to the regular PS5
Sony’s new Quick Spectral Super Resolution AI upscaling is coming first to Marvel’s Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei.
Sony’s new Quick Spectral Super Resolution AI upscaling is coming first to Marvel’s Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei.
Sony says that PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR), which is available on the PS5 Pro, “remains the gold standard,” and in Digital Foundry’s early hands-on with the tech, it does seem that QSSR isn’t as fast as PSSR because the PS5 doesn’t have dedicated machine learning silicon. As a result, you should probably expect closer to an upscaled 1440p resolution on PS5 instead of the upscaled 4K on PS5 Pro.
”On PS5 Pro, developers almost uniformly output to 4K and adjust render resolution beneath it,” Sony principal graphics R&D engineer Daniel Craig told Digital Foundry. “On PS5, teams have to be more flexible, tuning not just render resolution, but also their intermediate and final presentation targets depending on the graphics mode.”
But Craig also said that QSSR is “fundamentally a drop-in replacement for titles that already support PSSR” after only a few days of tuning, making it likelier that PS5 developers will take advantage. The tech will be “offered broadly to all PlayStation developers,” Sony says.
Marvel’s Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei will be the first games to take advantage of QSSR, and are getting patches today to offer the tech as “an additional graphics option on PS5.” (Ghost of Yōtei Complete Edition also launches today.) Here are a couple videos from Sony showing off how QSSR looks in those games, and it appears to make graphics a little bit sharper:
Digital Foundry writes that “the potential here is remarkable: low resolution and poor upscaling have impacted so many titles in this generation, but QSSR could make a big difference.”

title_en: Amazon releases its own Jev clone as decision models flood the web
title_fa: Amazon releases its own Jev clone as decision models flood the web
excerpt_en: Amazon Web Services' Strand Labs has released the latest Jevalike decision model, Strands Decider 2B.
excerpt_fa: Amazon Web Services' Strand Labs has released the latest Jevalike decision model, Strands Decider 2B.
content_en:
Amazon Web Services released an open source decision model inspired by TypeSafe’s Jev, with AI developers increasingly seeking intelligence that is more suited to computer automation than frontier LLMs.
Amazon’s Strands Decider 2B, released the same week OpenAI announced a similar offering, is a high-speed, low-cost way to sort between pre-decided options and deliver a measure of how confident it is in its choice. The model is fully open sourced, available now, and small enough to run locally.
Amazon distinguished engineer Marc Brooker came up with the project after seeing Jev and trying to build his own take on such a model. The homebrew project was successful enough — it briefly reached the top spot on the Jevbench ranking for models of its size — that Amazon engineers cleaned it up and released it as an offering from their Strands Labs, an organization developing new tools and protocols for deploying AI agents.
Brooker says the need for a tool like this emerged in conversations with AWS customers, whose agentic workflows didn’t always require the capability or cost of a fully featured LLM all the time.
“What originally piqued my interest in this class of models was that they make a perfect decider for a workflow step — ‘what is the next thing for me to do here, based on where I am?’” Brooker told TechCrunch. He said it offers customers “a workflow step that can be structured in a way that is more reliable, thanks to the confidence scores, thanks to the closed domain of answers, [and is] lower latency, potentially lower cost.”
Like other decision models, Strands Decider is built on the “torso” of an LLM, in this case Qwen3.5-2B, but instead of generating text, it delivers calibrated choices. TypeSafe named their model Jev after the economist William Stanley Jevons, with hopes of invoking his theory that the falling cost of something — like computer intelligence — can, in fact, increase its demand.
The fact that dozens of similar models have been produced by researchers since TypeSafe debuted its idea shows the wide interest, but also raises the question of how valuable they can be. Brooker suggests that the challenge will be in optimizing the model’s speedy decision-making without compromising its intelligence.
“There is a very careful balance to be found where you want to push its performance on accuracy and calibration on these kinds of tasks, without degrading its performance on understanding different languages, on having the kind of knowledge it has, which is what makes it general purpose and interesting and useful,” he told TechCrunch.
Still, he doesn’t necessarily expect the frontier labs to dominate the space, especially since, with smaller markets, the cost to build something interesting is in the hundreds or thousands of dollars.
For their part, TypeSafe executives say they are keeping their heads down and improving future models.
“I get that people think it’s a gold rush, but they might be underestimating the difficulty of making the models actually smart,” CEO and founder Diogo Almeida told TechCrunch, saying that for now, he didn’t see real competition for his company emerging yet.
“The current batch seems more like ML people wanting to implement a cool architecture than a team deeply dedicated to making intelligence useful.”

title_en: Shopify debuts Canvas, a way to build online stores by chatting with AI
title_fa: Shopify debuts Canvas, a way to build online stores by chatting with AI
excerpt_en: Shopify’s new Canvas site builder lets merchants create and customize their online stores by chatting with its AI agent Sidekick, while watching the changes happen in real time.
excerpt_fa: Shopify’s new Canvas site builder lets merchants create and customize their online stores by chatting with its AI agent Sidekick, while watching the changes happen in real time.
content_en:
Shopify introduced a new site-building tool Thursday called Canvas that lets merchants set up their Shopify store by chatting with AI. While Shopify already offered a fairly capable no-code builder before Canvas, it involved editing a selected theme by rearranging modular sections and blocks. Deeper customizations, however, would require editing code or bringing in a developer.
Now, with Canvas, merchants simply chat with Shopify’s AI agent, Sidekick, to create their site. As the AI makes changes, Canvas displays the results in real time, allowing merchants to see how the store looks overall as it comes together or zoom in to focus on certain details.
Notably, this isn’t a static preview, but the real code behind their store being rendered, according to Shopify. That means merchants can test the page’s full interactivity and animation, and view pages as they’d appear across different screen sizes. Sidekick also takes screenshots of the work so it can see the same thing the merchant sees as the site updates.
Canvas’s launch is part of a broader shift toward a future where building a website no longer requires coding it directly. It joins numerous other AI-powered site-building tools from companies like Wix, Squarespace, Webflow, and Framer, alongside vibe-coding platforms like Lovable and Replit.
Merchants can still click on individual elements to make changes directly, if they choose. But more likely, they’ll just tell Sidekick in a chat what they want to do.
Sidekick itself is not new, as it’s already been used to write code, build apps, customize themes, and make other edits. But it had yet to be pulled together into a full site-building product like Canvas, where users can see the entire store at once and zoom and pan around while making updates to the site’s actual files.
To make this work, Shopify gave Sidekick the ability to work directly with the theme’s files and simplified the theme architecture so the store’s structure, logic, and design would be easier for Sidekick to understand and change.
The product is in its early days, so there are areas where it will need to expand and improve. For instance, third-party theme support, app blocks and extensions, markets, translations, rollouts, and theme updates are all not part of the initial launch. Plus, Canvas is desktop-only. But the company told TechCrunch these are things the company plans to support over time; the product is just still new.
In the future, as it becomes more robust, Canvas could make becoming an online seller more accessible to those who don’t have the budget for developers and designers, or the time to learn to code.

title_en: California governor vetoes bill banning use of ‘pervert glasses’ to secretly record people
title_fa: California governor vetoes bill banning use of ‘pervert glasses’ to secretly record people
excerpt_en: The California state bill would have penalized people who secretly recorded people in public with wearables equipped with cameras and microphones.
excerpt_fa: The California state bill would have penalized people who secretly recorded people in public with wearables equipped with cameras and microphones.
content_en:
California Governor Gavin Newsom has used his veto authority to send a bill passed by the state’s legislature back to lawmakers, which would have made it unlawful to secretly record people with wearable recording devices.
Newsom said in a letter to lawmakers on Wednesday that he declined to sign the draft law, California Senate Bill 1130, on grounds that it defines wearable recording devices as “too broadly or imprecisely” and that this could lead to confusion and unintended consequences. Newsom added that the proposed bill also includes protections that already exist in California’s law.
The bill would have made California the first state to regulate the use of smart glasses, as countries like Norway seek to potentially ban the technology. Had California’s law passed, violators could face fines or prison time, while wearable makers that did not comply with the rules would have also faced fines.
The bill sought to prevent people from being recorded in public places without their explicit consent, amid a rising number of wearable products containing cameras and microphones that always listen and record everything nearby, like internet-connected glasses made by Meta and Snap. Meta sold more than 7 million wearable glasses last year alone. Several other hardware wearables, such as AI-powered pendants, have launched with mixed reactions.
The bill’s author, California state senator Eloise Gómez Reyes, was quoted by ABC News as saying that the bill aimed to help California respond to the rapid rollout of always-listening tech.
Critics and consumers alike have dubbed the controversial wearables “pervert glasses” following multiple reports of people recording and harassing people. Apple announced last month that its latest Apple Watch software will include an always-listening feature that allows wearers to replay a transcript of the past 15 seconds and also recap and summarize conversations from the day.

title_en: Audible thinks you want to have an AI-generated conversation with Dracula's beleaguered servant
title_fa: Audible thinks you want to have an AI-generated conversation with Dracula's beleaguered servant
excerpt_en: The platform is rolling out "Interactive Stories" starting with Bram Stoker's classic.
excerpt_fa: The platform is rolling out "Interactive Stories" starting with Bram Stoker's classic.
content_en:
Audible thinks you want to have an AI-generated conversation with Dracula's beleaguered servant
The platform is rolling out "Interactive Stories" starting with Bram Stoker's classic.
Audible just announced something called Interactive Stories, which lets listeners "become part of the story's world." This is done via generative AI, so people can sort of talk to a character. The first of these experiences will accompany the upcoming Audible Original adaptation of Bram Stoker's Dracula.
The Interactive Story involves Dracula's long-suffering servant Renfield. Audible says Renfield will assign the listener "a role, goal and stakes." The platform also promises that the "listener responds in their own words and the character reacts in real time." So it's some kind of LARP-ing type thing, which could be fun depending on how well it's done. The generative AI aspect doesn't give me much hope, but we'll have to wait and see.
"AI is allowing us to create new interactive experiences that today's listeners, especially younger audiences, are craving," said Andy Tsao, Chief Product and Analytics Officer at the company. A recent Pew Research survey seems to suggest that younger audiences are wary of AI, but maybe Audible has different data points as to what they're currently "craving."
The platform says this feature launches later this fall as a beta release. It didn't provide an official date, but that new audio adaptation of Dracula comes out on October 1. It'll probably happen sometime around then.
Audible has announced the next Interactive Story too. It's set in the world of the upcoming Exoplanet original audio novel. The experience was created alongside author Benjamin Percy, and that's set to release on November 5.

It visually displays who is speaking in real-time directly on the app and includes spoiler-free character cards. It can be tough to keep track of dozens of characters with an audiobook, as there's no visual reference.
This is already available with the platform's adaptation of George Orwell's 1984. It's also coming to Bram Stoker's Dracula and the aforementioned Exoplanet.

The platform says "listeners might glimpse a map" or be given the ability to "explore an image tied to a pivotal moment." A beta version of this feature will accompany The Cultural Tutor's Grand Tour: The Story of Europe in Six Cities, which is basically an audio tour of various historical destinations throughout the continent.

content_en:
I’m pretty sure I won’t be buying the $1,299 Meta VR Glasses. That’s too rich for my blood in today’s economy, and my feelings about Meta are… conflicted. But I want you to understand that Meta just changed the game. We’ve had glasses, but we’ve never had glasses like this.
Can VR glasses save VR?
Meta’s VR Glasses aren’t the glasses the industry promised. They might be better.
Meta’s VR Glasses aren’t the glasses the industry promised. They might be better.
The Meta VR Glasses are not an opaque VR headset. They are not a pair of transparent AR glasses. They might be the best of both. After playing with the Meta VR Glasses, Valve’s Steam Frame, the Apple Vision Pro, and the Google / Xreal Aura back to back, I think they’re the first design that could convince regular people to give VR a chance.
It’s not because they look like glasses. It’s not just that they’re five times lighter than a typical headset at around 100 grams. It’s certainly not the $1,300 price tag, even if that’s much less than a $3,700 Vision Pro.
It’s about what you see and feel — and what you don’t see and feel — when you put Meta’s VR Glasses on your head.
You aren’t fully enclosed. You aren’t isolated. Because the Meta VR Glasses are glasses, not goggles, you have real peripheral vision. You see a live video feed of your room in the center, thick “rims” around that, then an actual naked-eye view of your surroundings around those rims. Even when you’re in a game, you still have peripheral vision.
I know people who aren’t comfortable in VR at home because they can’t afford to feel isolated from their kids or pets. I’ve personally never felt comfortable wearing headsets on a plane or train or in a park because I don’t like being surrounded by strangers I can’t easily see.
Women have told me VR is a nonstarter because they have long hair or wear makeup. Many headsets balance their weight by sandwiching your head between a back strap and a front cushion, and they don’t want to deal with the hassle of a high ponytail or smears every time they strap in.
Glasses are a potential solution, resting on your ears and floating before your eyes instead of pushing on your head. For years, the industry has suggested headsets will eventually make way for glasses.
But typically when we talk about glasses, they’re transparent. We’re imagining indistinguishable-from-eyeglasses spectacles that let you see the real world in all its glory, then magically make virtual objects appear within the entirety of the frame.
Today’s transparent-display glasses have made leaps and bounds, but they’re not there yet. While the basic lenses might look like glasses and give you a glasses-like field of view, the displays inside the glasses light up a much smaller area. When I sweep my head left or right, up or down, I see virtual objects disappear even when I’m still looking roughly in their direction.
In 2013, I briefly wore Google Glass — a tiny screen above my right eye with a postage stamp-sized 15-degree diagonal field of view. In 2015, I tried Microsoft’s HoloLens, with a 34-degree field of view. Four years later, HoloLens 2 achieved 52 degrees diagonally, the Xreal One Pro glasses I’ve been testing offer 57 degrees, and the Xreal Aura will finally push transparent glasses to 70 degrees diagonal this fall.
But even with the Aura, 70 degrees diagonal is more like 60 degrees horizontal by 40 degrees vertical. Humans have roughly 120 degrees of binocular vision alone, and VR headsets like the Meta Quest 3 and Steam Frame offer around 110 degrees horizontal so you can feel like a virtual world is all around you.
Transparent glasses are also, well, transparent. Glasses like the Aura have to make their projected light compete with the real world while still letting you see through. That often means projectors right up against your brow. Virtual objects can seem ghostly unless you activate electrochromic lenses, which turn the clear lenses dark at the push of a button, blocking your view of the world.
Even then, you can see games, movies, and virtual desktops far better in a VR headset, where virtual light and real light don’t have to compete. You see the real world through what’s called “passthrough vision” — a live camera feed — with virtual objects realistically appearing at the correct depth and blocking real-life objects behind them.
That’s how the Steam Frame, Meta Quest, and Apple Vision Pro all work. But again, they weigh four to eight times as much and are fully enclosed. What if there were a lighter, open-air set of glasses that used passthrough vision instead of transparent lenses? You see where I’m going with this.
Instead of 60 degrees horizontal by 40 degrees vertical, the Meta VR Glasses offer 70 degrees by 66 degrees, and let me tell you, it feels like a bigger difference than it sounds. But the difference isn’t just the raw field of view — it’s that my real and virtual fields of view are the same. Anywhere I look inside the lenses, virtual objects can fill that frame, instead of getting abruptly cut off where the display part of the transparent display ends.
It also doesn’t hurt that the VR Glasses offer much higher angular resolution than most AR or VR devices (37ppd), making it easier to read text.
What you don’t get at 70 degrees by 66 degrees is full immersion. Some nerds like me will argue that the Meta VR Glasses don’t offer true VR, because it’s hard to feel like you’re “there” if you see so much less of your game. But it didn’t feel like I had tunnel vision, either, and it helps that the headset can track your hands far outside your field of view.
Wearing the Meta VR Glasses was the first time I thought to myself: Is there such a thing as “enough” field of view? I’ll always want more, but maybe the problem with virtual reality isn’t about feeling immersed. The industry’s problem is convincing enough people that it’s worth wearing any sort of headgear at all.

excerpt_fa: After nearly 18 years at LinkedIn and Microsoft, Ryan Roslansky is leaving the company. Roslansky, who until recently was the CEO of LinkedIn, was promoted to the head of Office last year and then took control of Microsoft Teams earlier this year. Roslansky's departure has...
content_en:
After nearly 18 years at LinkedIn and Microsoft, Ryan Roslansky is leaving the company. Roslansky, who until recently was the CEO of LinkedIn, was promoted to the head of Office last year and then took control of Microsoft Teams earlier this year. Roslansky’s departure has triggered another leadership shuffle inside Microsoft.
Microsoft’s Office and Teams chief is leaving
Ryan Roslansky is leaving after nearly 18 years at LinkedIn and Microsoft.
Ryan Roslansky is leaving after nearly 18 years at LinkedIn and Microsoft.
“Ryan leaves the organization in a strong position,” says Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella in an internal memo. “Over the past year, Ryan’s team has done critical work bringing together the product, engineering, and design foundations that have made this next phase possible.”
Roslansky is leaving a week after Microsoft announced its new Copilot, which the company is positioning as “the OS for work.” He’s also leaving around a month after calling fully AI-generated documents “a doom loop” for workers. “If we’re not careful, we’ll end up with a very expensive way to avoid writing and reading in an ocean of sameness, genericness,” said Roslansky in his LinkedIn post.
Microsoft is now moving the teams behind Office and Microsoft Teams over to Charles Lamanna, as part of the Copilot, Agents, and Platform (CAP) organization. This is the second major reshuffling of the Office teams after Rajesh Jha, former head of Microsoft’s experiences and devices group, retired from Microsoft earlier this year.
Microsoft’s chief design officer, Jon Friedman, is also moving to report to Copilot chief Jacob Andreou. Microsoft appointed Dan Shapero as its LinkedIn CEO earlier this year, and he will continue in this role and report directly to Nadella.
Roslansky describes the decision to leave Microsoft as a hard one in his own memo to his teams, and reveals he wasn’t willing to move to Microsoft’s Redmond headquarters full time. “I know what it would take for me to lead the next phase of this work well: being in Redmond full time, every day,” says Roslansky. “But my life and my family’s life are here in the Bay Area.”
Here’s Roslansky’s memo in full:
Team,
In 1996, as a college freshman, I taught myself to code so a few friends and I could help other students find a place to live around campus. I didn’t know much. I did know the internet was about to change how people found things, and I wanted to be as close to that as possible.
In 2009, Jeff Weiner made me his first hire at LinkedIn. I’ve spent the nearly 18 years since working on a much bigger version of that same idea: helping people find opportunity, and then helping them do great work once they have it.
This has (obviously) been the best professional experience of my life.
As a product manager, I got to build dozens of features that are still around today (some good, some not so good!). When I became CEO in 2020, the world was months into a pandemic that changed what work even meant. Nobody hands you a playbook for that. This team wrote one anyway. Since then, LinkedIn has passed a billion members and nearly tripled its business, and every bit of that belongs to the people who built it.
Last year, Satya asked me to help build the future of M365. Once again, the old rules didn’t apply. AI was rapidly changing how professionals work, and the world’s largest productivity suite needed to lead the way. That meant figuring out what Copilot, and the future of work, should look like as one ecosystem.
We still have a ways to go, but the progress over the past year has been inspiring to watch. A lot of talented people set aside their own roadmaps to make that happen. Thank you. I know it wasn’t easy.
Satya, thank you. When LinkedIn joined Microsoft, you gave us room to build, and then trusted many of us with a lot more. I’ve learned more from you than I can fit in an email, and I’m grateful for the friendship that came with it.
All of which made this a hard decision. I know what it would take for me to lead the next phase of this work well: being in Redmond full time, every day. But my life and my family’s life are here in the Bay Area. My wife Leigh gives her time to more local organizations than I can keep track of. Our youngest daughter just started high school, and our dog Buddy remains deeply committed to the trails on the Peninsula!
I thought about this for a long time. It’s the right call. The work now goes to leaders who are set up to take it further. I can’t wait to see what they do with it.
Over the years, people have asked me what’s kept me so energized and motivated in this work. I think the answer is that I got to spend my career working where doing good and doing well are the same thing. In technology, that’s the best place to operate.
Most companies start by focusing on doing well, so doing good becomes a compromise. It’s the last slide of the PowerPoint, or a separate .org. But when doing good is built into the product itself, it becomes a real competitive advantage. When we build valuable products, people find jobs, they hire, they learn skills, they start companies, they run companies. That creates value for members, customers and the world. And for our business too.
Not many companies get to work this way, and not many people get the chance to build something like it. We do.
That matters more now than it ever has. Technology will continue to touch every job on the planet, and the people building it will decide what kind of world it helps create. I can’t think of a better group to figure that out than the people reading this note.
Thank you for the best 18 years I could have asked for.
RR

title_en: Inside Microsoft’s big Copilot rethink
title_fa: Inside Microsoft’s big Copilot rethink
excerpt_en: Last week, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella hosted an intimate, invite-only event for leaders from some of its key enterprise customers. Instead of a flashy media event, Nadella outlined the future of Copilot directly to the customers Microsoft really cares about, pitching its latest...
excerpt_fa: Last week, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella hosted an intimate, invite-only event for leaders from some of its key enterprise customers. Instead of a flashy media event, Nadella outlined the future of Copilot directly to the customers Microsoft really cares about, pitching its latest...
content_en:
Last week, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella hosted an intimate, invite-only event for leaders from some of its key enterprise customers. Instead of a flashy media event, Nadella outlined the future of Copilot directly to the customers Microsoft really cares about, pitching its latest rethink of the AI assistant as the “OS for work.”
Inside Microsoft’s big Copilot rethink
Copilot is now being positioned as the ‘OS for work.’
Copilot is now being positioned as the ‘OS for work.’
Microsoft is adding coding and agent capabilities directly into Copilot, as well as bringing the full power of Office into Copilot for the first time. Nadella is betting that AI will change the way people work in the same way that Microsoft Office did in the ’80s and ’90s.
“How did a multinational company do a forecast in 1981? You had interoffice memos and faxes and all of these artifacts that then just disappeared and you suddenly had an Excel spreadsheet in an email,” said Nadella. “We are the architects of a new frontier of work, using these new tools and capabilities.”
Microsoft has spent the past few months fusing together its consumer and enterprise Copilot apps into a single unified user interface, with a goal to make Copilot as influential as Office once was. The result is a big departure from the Copilot consumer design that Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman launched two years ago. That design was heavily influenced by the work Inflection AI had done with the Pi personal AI assistant, after Microsoft hired many of the Inflection AI team just months prior.
The new Copilot app now looks a lot more like the commercial one, with separate tabs for chat, coding, and the new Autopilot AI agent. There are some small nods to the consumer UI that was available before, but overall it looks like the type of enterprise app you’d associate with Microsoft.
“There’s a really important reason why we decided to do this,” said Copilot chief Jacob Andreou at Microsoft’s customer-only event last week. “The bar for enterprise software is higher than it has ever been before. The expectations we have of the tools we adopt at work are set by the things we use after hours and at the weekends at home. What this means is that consumer UX and care needs to make its way into the workplace.”
Andreou joined Microsoft AI last year, focused on product and growth. In March, Nadella appointed him as the single boss of Copilot across both commercial and consumer, reporting directly to the Microsoft CEO. He’s now responsible for the design, engineering, and growth of Copilot.
Sources familiar with Microsoft’s Copilot plans tell me that redesigning Copilot over the last six months hasn’t been easy. There have been tensions between the team under Andreou, and those working for Charles Lamanna on the Copilot, Agents, and Platform (CAP) team. Lamanna’s team has been building Microsoft Scout, an always-on personal agent built on top of OpenClaw. Microsoft announced Scout at its Build developer conference in June, with just a desktop preview app. Less than six months later, I understand that the app has been put into maintenance mode, with Microsoft focusing on the cloud version, which has been rebranded to Autopilot.
I’m told the rebrand was driven in part by legal concerns around the Scout name, as Yahoo uses “Yahoo Scout” branding for its own AI-powered features. Sources tell me Microsoft had even considered using Mico, the Clippy-like character from the consumer Copilot, to replace Scout. Nadella favored Autopilot instead, allowing Microsoft to present its AI agent in a more enterprise-friendly way, instead of a bouncing blob.
Some of Microsoft’s caution around making Autopilot too cute comes at a time when rogue AI agents are hacking into businesses. Nadella addressed these concerns last week, laying out Microsoft’s design goals for Copilot. “[It’s] about organizations having control of their firms in an age of AI, where AI by definition is a learning machine,” said Nadella. “It can’t be about leaking the core of what your firm is about.”
Andreou also admitted that agents “have been almost impossible to bring into the enterprise,” due to them needing the autonomy and flexibility that businesses usually balk at. “It is their superpower, and it’s the same thing that makes them absolutely terrifying to an IT admin.”

title_en: Engadget's best of 2026
title_fa: Engadget's best of 2026
excerpt_en: The highest-rated devices that we reviewed this year in a variety of categories.

content_en:
Engadget's best of 2026
The highest-rated devices that we reviewed this year in a variety of categories.
By the end of the year, Engadget writers will complete over 150 product reviews. From Apple's iPhones to Google's Pixels, the AirPods to Sony's 1000X series and MacBooks to Dell's XPS, our reviews team covers a wide range of devices from a wide range of companies. During the course of the year, products that receive a score of 90 or higher earn Engadget's Editors' Choice, while other category-topping devices score in the high 80s.
Now that the year is coming to an end, we've compiled the highest-scoring products (so far) across a range of categories, along with commentary on each one from our writers, for our best of 2026.
Best Android phone: Google Pixel 11
Google's Pixel 11 is the definition of an iterative update. It looks essentially the same as the Pixel 10, and it has a similar camera array, a new Tensor G6 process, double the starting storage and a $100 price bump. But the Pixel 10 was so good that Google didn't need to reinvent the wheel this year. Refinements to a winning formula, some intelligent software updates and a gorgeous set of colors was enough to win me over.
The Pixel 11 is one of few smartphones in its class to have three camera lenses on the back, including a capable 5x telephoto. That's something you can't get in the otherwise-comparable iPhone 17, and it bests the 3x camera on Samsung's Galaxy S26. Getting a telephoto camera on a phone that costs less than $1,000 is a trick Google may have first pulled last year, but it's still a big deal.
Many of the software tricks Google added this year, like Rambler (which turns your, well, rambling dictation into clearer and more concise text) and Proactive Suggestions (which nudge you to do things like add items to your calendar based on your conversations) are genuinely useful as well. Add in outstanding build quality, fast performance and long battery life and the Pixel 11 does just about anything that most smartphone buyers could want. — Nathan Ingraham, Deputy News Editor
Best iPhone: Apple iPhone 18 Pro
Of all the iPhones introduced in 2026, the iPhone 18 Pro was the clear choice. Due to a change in Apple's product release strategy this year, there were only three iPhone models to consider: the iPhone 17e, iPhone 18 Pro (and Pro Max) and the iPhone Duo. We haven't been able to review the last one yet, so it's not eligible. Plus, the fact that it's a first-generation product with a hefty price means it's unlikely to be the right device for most people, anyway.
That said, though the iPhone 17e is a solid phone for the cost, the title of best iPhone almost by default goes to the iPhone 18 Pro. It simply offers the top-tier combination of features for the money.
Its overall package of updates seems incremental, but the iPhone 18 Pro served up some compelling new hardware. Variable aperture and pro camera controls are useful for manual photographers, while things like the sensor-signed Apple Reference Image authentication are a convenient and simple addition that can help educate a larger audience on how to tell if a photo has been manipulated.
Throw in a smaller, more functional Dynamic Island, improved thermal management and faster battery charging, the iPhone 18 Pro starts to look more beefy. Plus, the new burgundy and blue color options are quite droolworthy. If you're looking for an Apple handset with the best performance and cameras, the iPhone 18 Pro is the easy pick. — Cherlynn Low, Executive Editor
Best affordable laptop: Apple MacBook Neo
Apple seemingly did the impossible with the MacBook Neo: It somehow delivered a $600 budget laptop that didn't feel too different from a premium notebook like the MacBook Air. Even though it's $100 more now, thanks to the ongoing AI-induced RAM crisis, the MacBook Neo is still a tremendous deal. It's fast enough for everyday computing tasks (even with just 8GB of RAM), its screen is bright enough to use in direct sunlight and it features an excellent keyboard and trackpad.
The MacBook Neo is such a trendsetter, now every PC maker is rushing to copy Apple's formula. But there's still nothing else that offers the same combination of premium build quality and components on the Windows side. — Devindra Hardawar, Senior Reporter
Best macOS laptop: Apple MacBook Air M5
The MacBook Air remains one of the best ultraportables on the market thanks to its combination of speed (now with Apple's M5 chip), premium build quality and portability. Sure, there are lighter Windows laptops now, but they're not as performant as Apple's hardware, and they often deliver a worse user experience.
The MacBook Air is the complete package. It's fast enough to handle just about everything you throw at it, including light gaming and video editing. It's sturdy enough to last years. And it's also completely silent, since it has no cooling fan. While Windows notebooks are now offering sleek OLED screens at this price range, PC makers still struggle to match the quality of the MacBook Air's keyboard, trackpad, speakers and battery life. — D.H.
Best gaming laptop: ASUS ROG Zephyrus Duo
The ASUS ROG Zephyrus Duo is big, heavy and has one of the most bombastic designs we've seen on any gaming laptop in recent history. But that's exactly what makes it so awesome. Sure, it's ridiculously expensive starting at — wait for it — $4,500, but it has everything you could want in a bleeding edge gaming PC, and then some. It features not one but two 3K OLED displays, a fully detachable keyboard, as much as 64GB of RAM and support for up to an RTX 5090 GPU.
You also get surprisingly punchy speakers and a ton of ports, including a total of four USB slots, a full-size HDMI jack and an SD card reader. And for something this powerful, its battery life isn't half bad either. Really, this thing is closer to a portable battle station than a basic gaming notebook, and if you can stomach its price, there isn't really anything else...

title_en: Samsung suddenly jacks up the prices of Galaxy S26 phones
title_fa: Samsung suddenly jacks up the prices of Galaxy S26 phones
excerpt_en: RAMageddon comes for us all.
excerpt_fa: RAMageddon comes for us all.
content_en:
Samsung suddenly jacks up the prices of Galaxy S26 phones
Most got a $100 increase while the 1TB Galaxy S26 Ultra jumped up by $200 to $2,000.
Samsung has increased the prices of its Galaxy S26, S26+ and S26 Ultra phones by at least $100 on its website, even though most configurations were already more expensive than last year's equivalents when they debuted in March. The S26 FE, which the company released a month ago, is the only one of the current slate-style smartphones that avoided a sudden price increase.
Unless you go with an FE or wait for a sale (Black Friday is fast approaching and Amazon's Prime Big Deal Days is next week), it'll now cost you at least $1,000 to pick up a Galaxy S26 phone. That's the price for the base model with 256GB of storage, meaning that particular flavor of the Galaxy S26 is now $200 more than its Galaxy S25 equivalent.
If you want a Galaxy S26 with 512GB of storage, that'll now run you $1,200. The Galaxy S26+ is $1,200 for 256GB of storage and $1,400 for the 512GB variant. As for the Galaxy S26 Ultra, you'll need to pay $1,400 for 256GB of storage, $1,600 for 512GB and $2,000 for 1TB. That last one stands out since Samsung increased the price by $200, rather than $100 for the other variants.
Even though S26 prices were higher and its revenue grew overall, Samsung's mobile division posted its first-ever loss for the April-June quarter of this year. It pinned a decline in operating profit on higher costs and components like RAM and storage becoming more expensive. That's most likely why the company jacked up the S26 prices again. (Engadget has contacted Samsung for clarification).
On the contrary, Samsung's chip division is doing gangbusters. It helped drive the company overall to all-time high quarterly revenue and operating profit in its second fiscal quarter.
This may not be the end of Samsung's smartphone price hikes, either. Reports suggest the company may make storage upgrades even more expensive in the S27 lineup.

title_en: One year later, Tesla and Musk still don’t have a good definition of ‘abundance’
title_fa: One year later, Tesla and Musk still don’t have a good definition of ‘abundance’
excerpt_en: The CEO promised to get more specific about his vision. But the details are still absent.
excerpt_fa: The CEO promised to get more specific about his vision. But the details are still absent.
content_en:
On September 1, 2025, Elon Musk laid out his fourth “Master Plan” for Tesla, which was immediately criticized by some of his most ardent fans for being generic. Musk agreed and promised to add more specifics.
They never came. But that hasn’t stopped Musk and other Tesla executives from spending much of the past year promising that the company’s many futuristic efforts — robotaxis, robots, AI — are all part of a grander machine that will create an era of “amazing abundance.”
What that means, more than a year later, is still tricky to pin down.
The topline promises of the plan have remained big and bawdy even as its tagline has changed from sustainable abundance — a clearer connection to the company’s former mission — to the “amazing abundance” slogan, which Musk chose because it was “more joyful.”
Musk has talked about a far-flung future where robots and AI do surgery and increase access to medical care.
He has said the proliferation of AI and robotics means that “everyone can have a penthouse if they want.” He (virtually) shouted “Amazing abundance for all!” in a quote-tweet of a post from Midjourney founder David Holz, who had claimed 5 million humanoid robots could “build Manhattan in ~6 months.” In July, Musk told Economist editor-in-chief Zanny Minton Beddoes that amazing abundance means “anyone can have anything they can think of.”
He also mentioned on Joe Rogan’s podcast late last year that “sustainable abundance” would mean “we haven’t destroyed nature” or “paved the rainforest” and we still “have the national parks,” despite supporting two politicians — Donald Trump and Jair Bolsonaro — who have actively worked against those goals. He appears to have only made this particular claim once, though.
Practical details are basically nonexistent, though. Does Musk really think that people want to build three billion nearly-empty apartment buildings with an average of two to three tenants to each lone penthouse? He doesn’t say.
Tesla and Musk didn’t respond to requests for comment.
While some of these ideas sound like the kind of proclamations uttered after a hearty bong rip in freshman housing, Tesla hasn’t treated them as frivolous. Quite the opposite: Master Plan IV became a central justification for handing Musk a $1 trillion pay package in 2025.
Tesla has said in regulatory filings that the “product goals” in that comp package — 20 million vehicles delivered, 10 million active subscriptions to Full Self-Driving, and deploying one million each of its robotaxis and robots — play a “key role” in supporting Musk’s “vision” of abundance. Tesla’s chair Robyn Denholm called this out in a letter to shareholders after they approved the $1 trillion plan last November.
“[Y]ou support the vision embodied by Master Plan Part IV and want us to keep steering Tesla toward the extraordinary future we all see ahead,” Denholm wrote. “A world that is not ‘zero-sum’ but instead one in which we can and will accelerate global prosperity for all by creating a safer, cleaner and more enjoyable world. In a year when many tried to sow doubt and negativity, you chose a better future.”
Further down in that letter, Denholm lionized Tesla shareholders for having “reaffirmed” their “belief in a trailblazer who has turned Tesla into one of the most valuable companies in history and who continues to push humanity closer to a future of sustainable abundance for all.”
Denholm said this was “not just a slogan,” but that it “is about bringing about the best future you can imagine.” Of course, Musk’s reworked version is definitely a slogan. In August, Tesla applied to trademark “amazing abundance” to be used for all sorts of things, from cars and robots to stickers, bags, cups, and even bottle openers.
Perhaps Musk and Tesla have kept things broad because, when pushed even slightly, the world’s richest man acknowledges some limits. In a November 2025 conference appearance, Musk said Tesla’s robots “will be able to make anyone a house,” or even a castle — “as long as you don’t just insist on it being in a particular location.”
Desirable locations are a finite resource in a world with 8 billion people, especially as the globe heats up and some places become inhospitable to human life — a problem Tesla spent years nominally trying to solve, until Musk changed the mission last year.

title_en: Brian Chesky interview: AI agents need their own operating system
title_fa: Brian Chesky interview: AI agents need their own operating system
excerpt_en: Brian Chesky on making Airbnb agent-friendly, the state of consumer AI, and why the world needs an AI-native operating system.
excerpt_fa: Brian Chesky on making Airbnb agent-friendly, the state of consumer AI, and why the world needs an AI-native operating system.
content_en:
Airbnb rolled out its new AI-powered search this week as part of its fall update, a significant step for a company that has been slow and deliberate about AI. Co-founder and CEO Brian Chesky has said in the past that a chatbot-only interface is not fit for travel discovery. With more AI on the way to the Airbnb app, I caught up with Chesky over Zoom to talk about how the company is approaching it, where interfaces are headed, why consumer AI still isn’t working, and what role voice will play.
Chesky hasn’t changed his mind on chatbots. His thesis is that apps have not always been interoperable unless companies struck a business deal. On the other hand, agents are like “apps with faces,” and when they talk to each other, all apps can become interoperable.

title_en: Newsom vetoes smart glasses privacy bill
title_fa: Newsom vetoes smart glasses privacy bill
excerpt_en: The language of the bill was overbroad, in Newsom's opinion.
excerpt_fa: The language of the bill was overbroad, in Newsom's opinion.
content_en:
Newsom vetoes smart glasses privacy bill
The law would have banned people from using wearables to secretly record others in private areas of businesses.
Gavin Newsom, the governor of California, has vetoed a bill that would have prohibited people from secretly record others using smart glasses in certain spaces. Those would have included changing rooms and doctors' offices, as the Associated Press notes.
In addition, SB-1130 would have forced the manufacturers of wearables to include an indicator that's on when the devices are recording video or audio (many already do). It would also have banned the sale of tech designed to mask a recording light or sound.
As Newsom put it, "this bill would make it a misdemeanor to operate a wearable recording device to capture sound or video of any other person in any area within a place of business where the person has a reasonable expectation of privacy." He wrote in a letter to the State Senate that certain language used in the bill was too broad. "For example, the bill's definition of 'wearable recording device' could include certain smartwatches or other worn devices widely used in public spaces and capable of recording which could lead to significant confusion and unintended consequences," Newsom added.
As the governor pointed out, California already bans people from using an electronic device to record others in areas where they have a reasonable expectation of privacy. Like some other states, it has a two-party consent law that requires both participants of a conversation (including over the phone) to agree for it to be recorded. Still, more specific legal language could have helped deter people from violating others' privacy using smart glasses. There's a reason why many folks refer to these devices as "pervert glasses," after all.
TechNet, an advocacy group representing a litany of notable tech companies, opposed the law. Had it come into effect, someone found guilty of secretly recording others would have faced fines of up to $1,500 and/or a prison sentence. Companies making wearables without a recording indicator or tech designed to block such indicators would have faced fines of up to $2,500 per violation.

title_en: Japanese court rules human voices are protected in landmark AI case
title_fa: Japanese court rules human voices are protected in landmark AI case
excerpt_en: Humans vs AI: It's time to d-d-d-d-duel.
excerpt_fa: Humans vs AI: It's time to d-d-d-d-duel.
content_en:
Japanese court rules human voices are protected in landmark AI case
An anime voice actor was partly successful in his case against an anonymous TikTok account.
A Tokyo court has sided with a Japanese voice actor who claimed a TikTok account had used AI to clone his "lustrous" baritone delivery, ruling that the human voice is protected by law in a landmark case.
Kenjiro Tsuda is a prominent anime voice actor who has starred in huge number of movies, series and video games across his more than 30-year career, with his turn as Seto Kaiba in Yu-Gi-Oh! arguably being his most iconic role. Tsuda asserted that the voice of the narrator of several TikTok videos uploaded to an anonymous account between July 2024 and the second half of last year was cloned from his own voice. While he was partially victorious in the case, his request to order TikTok to remove the videos in question was dismissed, as the offending account has already been deleted.
In its decision, the court said that using the voice of an actor without permission should be deemed an infringement on their publicity rights, as reported by AFP. This was the first case of its kind in Japan.
Tsuda argued that the tell was the unmistakably deep and "lustrous" nature of the AI-generated vocal delivery in the narration. The actor's legal team said the account's popularity — at its height it had more than 200,000 followers — was due to the novelty of its "dubious, sordid content" being narrated by a prominent star. TikTok responded in court by arguing that a "generic male voice" whose similarity to Tsuda's was debatable was used in the narration, according to court records seen by AFP.
The Japanese government has been notably pro-AI in its national strategy, but there is growing concern among anime voice actors that more needs to be done to protect the creators whose work (or likeness) is often ingested by this technology. Last year, Japan's government asked OpenAI to ensure that anime and manga content it deemed to be "irreplaceable treasures" were not being used to train the company's Sora 2 generator in a way that violates copyright.

title_en: NYC is now the first city in America that bans sketchy subscriptions
title_fa: NYC is now the first city in America that bans sketchy subscriptions
excerpt_en: New York City residents struggling to get out of recurring subscription fees can now submit complaints to the city government. As of Thursday, the city's click-to-cancel rule has taken effect, which requires businesses to make it as easy to cancel a subscription as it is to sign...
excerpt_fa: New York City residents struggling to get out of recurring subscription fees can now submit complaints to the city government. As of Thursday, the city's click-to-cancel rule has taken effect, which requires businesses to make it as easy to cancel a subscription as it is to sign...
content_en:
New York City residents struggling to get out of recurring subscription fees can now submit complaints to the city government. As of Thursday, the city’s click-to-cancel rule has taken effect, which requires businesses to make it as easy to cancel a subscription as it is to sign up. That means a gym that lets you join online, for example, can’t make you call or go in person to end your subscription.
NYC is now the first city in America that bans sketchy subscriptions
A new consumer portal promises not to send complaints into a “chatbot doom loop.”
A new consumer portal promises not to send complaints into a “chatbot doom loop.”
It’s the first municipality to see the rule take effect, after an appeals court struck down a federal version for procedural issues. The city expects it to save New Yorkers anywhere from $21.5 million to $162.5 million annually. And to NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP) Commissioner Samuel Levine, it’s an example of how state and local governments can hold companies accountable when federal efforts fail. “No one should need 45 minutes of hold music to stop paying for something they never wanted,” NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement. “If a company can take your money with one click, you should be able to get your money back with one click. And now, if they won’t let you cancel, the City is coming for them.”
Levine was the Federal Trade Commission consumer protection chief under Lina Khan, and he tried to usher in the click-to-cancel rule at a national level. He says the experience of implementing the rule in NYC has been “night and day.”
“We proposed this rule this year. We finalized it this year. It’s taking effect this year. This is the speed of government as it should be,” Levine tells The Verge in an exclusive interview. While Levine says he’s proud of his work on the FTC rule and sees it as a “model” for other state and local governments, “at the end of the day, it took more than four years. And then after all of that, it never actually gave Americans the relief they needed.” While the FTC under current Chair Andrew Ferguson has taken an initial step toward potentially reestablishing a similar rule, Levine is betting that more municipalities will do so first. While that leaves fewer Americans protected, it still creates a deterrent for businesses to engage in deceptive subscription practices.
“This is the speed of government as it should be”
In New York, consumers can use a new portal to file complaints if they believe a business gave them unclear subscription terms, delayed cancellation, or failed to inform them the subscription would auto-renew. After filing a complaint, DCWP will review it and could reach out for more information and try to get consumers’ money back and help them cancel relevant subscriptions. If the agency sees a pattern of noncompliance at a certain business, it could prompt further investigation and legal action. Under the rule, businesses could face fines starting at $525 per violation.
The mayor’s Public Interest Technology (PIT) Crew built the portal in 10 weeks; Levine assures consumers that the experience will be far different from the White House’s newly launched America.gov, which he says appears to be “just an AI chatbot layered on top of the federal government’s existing infrastructure.” When consumers submit a complaint to the click-to-cancel portal, Levine says, “they’re not going to be diverted into a chatbot doom loop. We’re going to have actual people whose full-time job is to help them.”
He also says it won’t be like going to a DMV office to renew your driver’s license. “If we want to restore people’s faith in government and the ability of government to deliver, we need to show that government can create excellent products. We need to show that every experience is not going to the DMV. And I mean, no offense to our colleagues at the DMV,” Levine says. “People have really bad associations with interacting with the government, and sometimes that deters them from filing complaints. You can have the best laws in the world, but at the end of the day, if your eyes and ears, the people you’re working to protect, don’t want to actually deal with the government and tell us what happened, those laws are not going to be effective.”
Update October 1st: Added statement from NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

title_en: Photon held a funeral for mobile apps. Now it has $4.5M to help replace them with agents.
title_fa: Photon held a funeral for mobile apps. Now it has $4.5M to help replace them with agents.
excerpt_en: The startup helps developers build AI agents that work over iMessage, SMS/RCS, email, and other messaging platforms. It's a bet that consumers will increasingly use agents instead of downloading apps.
excerpt_fa: The startup helps developers build AI agents that work over iMessage, SMS/RCS, email, and other messaging platforms. It's a bet that consumers will increasingly use agents instead of downloading apps.
content_en:
The AI startup Photon is so sure that agents will eventually come to replace mobile apps that it held a funeral for the latter — yes, a real funeral in a church, with speeches and everything. Photon, which helps developers build agents that work over iMessage and WhatsApp, now has $4.5 million in seed funding to develop its products. The raise comes after the company signed up over 40,000 developers and grew its revenue 10x in just four months, it says.
Photon co-founder and CEO Daniel Tian said the “app funeral,” held in San Francisco on September 17, was also a developer day for the startup, featuring panels from Vercel, Stripe, and OpenAI. It also included an actual coffin for app icons.
The move to host an app funeral was obviously somewhat tongue-in-cheek, but Tian believes the app era is coming to an end. “Honestly, it’s going to take a while, but I think, directionally, it’s inevitable,” he said of the shift from apps to agents.
The thesis behind the startup, as you may have guessed, is that users no longer want to install new apps. Instead, they want access to agents that work through the messaging apps they already use, like iMessage and WhatsApp.
Meta’s Muse, whose app has soared to No. 1 on the app stores, is putting that theory to the test. But even if Muse comes to dominate the consumer AI space, Tian sees a market for serving developers who want their applications to work over messaging services. That’s why Photon is offering a package of tools, including a unified API, an extensible channel framework, a command-line interface (CLI), and an observability suite. Combined, they allow developers to build and operate an agent experience that works over iMessage, WhatsApp, Telegram, SMS or RCS, email, voice, and more.
The idea for Photon emerged from the time co-founders Tian and Ryan Zhu, the CTO, spent building consumer apps as students, often at hackathons. Every time they finished a new app, they hit the same bottleneck: getting people to discover it. By building an agent that worked within iMessage, they realized they could reach people through an app those people already use every day: Apple’s Messages.
Tian, for instance, had built a bot that would text his friends back as him over iMessage. When he and Zhu made the technology open source on GitHub, thousands of developers adopted it. So they went all in. Tian dropped out of UPenn’s M&T program, and Zhu left high school, later becoming a visiting student at MIT’s Media Lab.
Today, the open source version of Photon still accounts for 98% of its use.
This April, the founders decided to create a managed platform and sell access to it via subscription tiers. This hosted version of the product offers 99.95% uptime, which is much higher than what you’d get if you were just running the open source version on your local Mac for a hobby project. It’s also SOC 2 Type II and HIPAA-compliant, which opens the door to healthcare agent use cases.
To date, the startup’s platform has attracted over 40,000 developer sign-ups and now includes paying clients. (Any usage beyond 10 users requires moving out of the free tier to one of the three paid tiers, we’re told.) The company isn’t sharing revenue figures but said that, in addition to the 10x revenue growth, it’s seeing less than 3% churn, and its messaging volume has grown by 5x in the last month alone.
Customers using Photon include Corgi Insurance; social introductions app Boardy; Gen Z dating platform Ditto; business banking platform Rho; finance AI assistant Fliptexts; AI email client Slashy; and others building agents for fintech, consumer AI, and other vertical use cases.
Photon’s technology integration partners also include companies such as Vercel (Eve and ChatSDK) and Nous Research, whose Hermes agent uses Photon as its default iMessage layer. title_en: Hearing tech startup Legato launches its AI hearing glasses
title_fa: Hearing tech startup Legato launches its AI hearing glasses
excerpt_en: The glasses stem from the startup’s goal of making hearing care more accessible by addressing the cost, comfort, and stigma associated with traditional hearing aids.
excerpt_fa: The glasses stem from the startup’s goal of making hearing care more accessible by addressing the cost, comfort, and stigma associated with traditional hearing aids.
content_en:
Hearing tech startup Legato announced on Thursday that its flagship AI-based hearing glasses are now available for purchase. The glasses, called Legato Frames, integrate the company’s patented hearing-assistance technology into the arms of eyewear frames. Starting at $999, Legato Frames are designed for adults with up to moderate levels of hearing loss.
The glasses stem from the startup’s goal of making hearing care more accessible by addressing the cost, comfort, and stigma associated with traditional hearing aids.
Unlike traditional hearing aids, which often use directional microphones to focus on sounds coming from a particular direction and can struggle in noisy environments, Legato takes a different approach. Its AI-powered system distinguishes voices from background noise and amplifies voices while reducing unwanted sounds.
While the frames have an open-ear design, sound isn’t broadcast to people around you. The frames feature a dual-speaker system that directs sound toward the wearer while canceling sound that escapes, reducing sound by 99% just a few inches away from the ear.
All processing happens directly on the glasses, with no cameras or recording, the company says.
The glasses weigh 34 grams with lenses and offer 10-12 hours of battery life. Legato Frames are available in three styles and support prescription lenses and Bluetooth streaming for music and calls.
The official launch of the glasses comes a few weeks after the startup emerged from stealth with $12 million in funding from Neotribe Ventures, Listen, and Village Global.
Legato was founded in 2024 by Mehul Trivedi and Steve Romine, who bring deep experience in wearables and hearing care from Bose, where Trivedi led the creation of Bose Frames and Romine ran the hearing aids division. After their time at Bose, Trivedi joined EssilorLuxottica, where he led smart eyewear efforts and worked on the Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses, while Romine went on to serve as COO of hearing care company Audicus. The pair then joined forces to explore the intersection of hearing technology and smart eyewear.
Legato Frames can be purchased on the startup’s website or through select eye care providers in the U.S., where they are eligible for coverage by vision insurance.

title_en: Audible’s new features let you explore book worlds — and use AI to talk to characters
title_fa: Audible’s new features let you explore book worlds — and use AI to talk to characters
excerpt_en: Audible is rolling out new features that help listeners keep track of characters, explore places and imagery mentioned in books, and even interact with characters using generative AI.
excerpt_fa: Audible is rolling out new features that help listeners keep track of characters, explore places and imagery mentioned in books, and even interact with characters using generative AI.
content_en:
Facing new competition in the audiobook market from Spotify, Audible is turning to AI and other technology to enhance the listening experience. On Thursday, the Amazon-owned company introduced three new features that will allow listeners to explore a book’s characters, engage in interactive stories, and view additional imagery and bonus information about landmarks or places mentioned in the book.
If you’re thinking the last would be great for highlighting the different courts’ locations in Sarah J. Maas’ faerie realm of Prythian, I must disappoint you. The feature will first arrive in just one title for now, “The Cultural Tutor: A Modern Guide to History, Art and Philosophy in 49 Short Chapters” by Sheehan Quirke, which focuses on making culture more accessible by teaching about poetry, art, architecture, geography, and more in short lessons.
The other new features, a character guide and interactive stories, are also starting off fairly small.
With Audible’s October 1 release of its Audible Original “Dracula,” the character guide will help listeners keep track of the cast of characters in the book, something that’s harder to do when listening than when reading. (The Audible Originals label doesn’t necessarily signal that the content is original, as “Dracula” is not. It means Audible’s own studios have produced the audiobook, memoir, exclusive series, podcast, or performance.)
In “Dracula,” the character guide will display who’s speaking in real time directly on the player page so listeners don’t get lost. It will also provide spoiler-free character cards, which showcase the narrator behind the voice and their bio. Audible says users will later be able to interact with the guide to ask questions about the story as it unfolds.
Other audiobooks gaining access to the character guide include the Audible Original of George Orwell’s “1984” and the forthcoming Audible Original “Exoplanet” from writer Benjamin Percy and executive producer Andy Weir (author of “Project Hail Mary” and “The Martian”).
A third feature, interactive stories, will also come to “Dracula” and “Exoplanet.”
Here, the idea is to bring the listener into the story through a bonus experience in which they interact with a book’s character. Powered by generative AI, the feature lets listeners interact with Dracula’s servant, Renfield, in the new Audible Original.
The character will speak first, giving the listener a role, goal, and stakes, and the listener then responds in their own words. The character will react to what’s said in real time.
Audible says the creators are involved in the foundations of the interactive stories, so the stories stay grounded in what’s happening in the book. Or, in the case of something like “Dracula,” the stories are meant to stay faithful to the original creator’s vision.
The changes come as audiobook listenership and revenue grow, with U.S. sales reaching $2.43 billion in 2025. The increased demand can be chalked up to several factors, from the proliferation of the smartphone to people’s increasingly busy schedules that make sitting down to read a book feel like a luxury. One could probably also credit TikTok’s “BookTok” community for pushing reading more into the mainstream — something that’s reflected in the most popular audiobook genres, which overlap with BookTok’s interests in fiction, sci-fi, thrillers, and, of course, romantasy.
“These new features invite listeners into a story in ways that simply weren’t possible before, marking the latest step in our nearly 30-year journey to push audio storytelling forward,” said Audible’s Chief Content Officer Rachel Ghiazza in a statement about the launch. “We’re excited to build on these while working hand in hand with creators, because we know that more time spent with stories benefits everyone who helps bring them to life.”
The company says the features are currently in a beta test, and the plan is to expand to more titles over time.

title_en: The new Kindle ditches the raised bezel in a push toward a smaller, lighter e-reader
title_fa: The new Kindle ditches the raised bezel in a push toward a smaller, lighter e-reader
excerpt_en: The new Kindle lineup features its lightest and thinnest designs yet, with a sleek, front-flush display that eliminates bezels for good.
excerpt_fa: The new Kindle lineup features its lightest and thinnest designs yet, with a sleek, front-flush display that eliminates bezels for good.
content_en:
Amazon is giving the Kindle its most significant physical redesign in years, introducing a refreshed lineup of e-readers built around a deceptively simple idea: getting rid of the raised bezel.
The redesigned Kindle unveiled Thursday replaces the traditional raised bezel surrounding the display with a flush-front design, creating a cleaner, more seamless look. But bezels also give readers a place to rest their fingers without accidentally touching the screen and triggering a page turn or another touchscreen command. Amazon says it has designed around that problem.
At a press briefing, Kevin Keith, Amazon’s vice president of devices, said the company is using “Cap” (capacitive) touch technology and haptics to create what he describes as a “dead zone.” As a reader grips the Kindle, the device detects where a finger is resting and adjusts the touch-sensitive area accordingly.
“When you’re gripping the Kindle, wherever you put your thumb, it will self-detect a dead zone in the Cap touch. It will just readjust, and it’ll know that the finger is there,” Keith said.
Alongside the bezel-free redesign, the standard six-inch Kindle is now 6.8 millimeters thick and weighs 140 grams, making it both thinner and lighter than its predecessor. Amazon is positioning it as the most pocket-friendly Kindle in the lineup.
Amazon said the new display is also 30% faster at page turns than the previous generation. The lineup also introduces new colors, including Ube, Alpine Sky, Seaglass Green, Graphite, and Fig.
The new Kindle starts at $149.99 and is available in Ube and Graphite. For the first time, Amazon is also offering an aluminum-backed version, with 32GB of storage and color options, including Alpine Sky and Seaglass Green.
The redesign extends to the Kindle Paperwhite, which is also thinner and lighter than the previous generation.
Amazon describes the Paperwhite as having the largest display in the Kindle lineup, along with the highest contrast ratio. The company says the combination is designed to deliver “deep blacks and crisp text, and images that pop off the screen, whether you’re reading in bright sunlight or under the covers at night.”
The standard Paperwhite comes with 16GB of storage and costs $199.99 in Graphite. A 32GB Signature Edition costs $249.99 and is available in Graphite and Seaglass Green.
The Kindle Colorsoft, which Amazon introduced in 2024 as its first Kindle with a color display, also adopts the thinner, lighter, flush-front design used across the refreshed lineup. The standard Colorsoft has 16GB of storage and starts at $289.99 in Graphite. A 32GB Signature Edition is available in Graphite and Fig for $319.99.
The new Kindle and its aluminum version are available starting today in the U.S., Canada, Mexico, Brazil, the U.K., Germany, France, Italy, Spain, Ireland, the Netherlands, Belgium, Sweden, Poland, Japan, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Egypt, and Australia.
The new Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Colorsoft are available for preorder across the same regions.
Amazon is also continuing to offer its Kids lineup. The Kids Kindle is currently available for purchase, whereas the Kids Kindle Colorsoft is available for preorder in the U.S., Canada, the U.K., Germany, and Japan.
